trap.wrong: "Kafka supports exactly-once, so we're covered end to end."
trap.why: Exactly-once covers Kafka topics and Flink state. Database writes, API calls and emails are repeated on replay unless they're idempotent.
trap.probe: Processing vs delivery, transactions with read_committed, two-phase-commit sinks, and what you still own.
trap.say: "Exactly-once processing inside Kafka and Flink; any external sink needs deterministic idempotency keys because replay will repeat it."

thesis: Kafka and Flink give exactly-once processing within their boundary: idempotent producers, transactions and checkpointed state make each record's effect on Kafka topics and Flink state happen once. Side effects outside that boundary (databases, APIs, emails) are still your job: make them idempotent or transactional with the checkpoint.
pitch: Delivery over a network is at least once; what systems provide is exactly-once effect. Kafka's idempotent producer removes duplicates from producer retries per partition. Kafka transactions let a consume-transform-produce application atomically write output records and commit its consumer offsets, so downstream consumers reading with read_committed isolation see each result once. Flink checkpoints its state and source offsets consistently; on failure it rewinds to the last checkpoint and reprocesses, and its two-phase-commit sinks, including the Kafka sink, commit output only when a checkpoint completes. What you still own: any sink that isn't transactional with Flink or Kafka, such as a database write, an HTTP call to a partner, or an email. On replay after failure those happen again, so they need idempotency keys or upserts keyed by a deterministic id. Also, consumers reading with read_uncommitted see aborted data, and exactly-once adds latency, because output becomes visible only at transaction or checkpoint commit.

points.d: Exactly-once processing (effects applied once) not exactly-once delivery. Records may be read and processed more than once internally; the system makes the visible result as if once.
Producer id plus sequence numbers per partition let the broker discard duplicate writes from retries.
Atomically write to multiple partitions and commit consumer offsets. Consumers with read_committed see only committed transactions.
Consistent snapshots of operator state and source positions. After a failure, the job restores state and replays input from the checkpointed offsets.
Flink sinks that support it pre-commit output during a checkpoint and commit when the checkpoint completes. Output visibility is tied to checkpoint frequency.
External side effects: database writes, API calls, emails, payments. Make them idempotent (upsert by deterministic key, idempotency keys) because replay will repeat them.
Latency equal to checkpoint or transaction interval for visible output, more coordination overhead, and careful configuration (isolation level, transaction timeouts).

decision: Use Kafka transactions or Flink exactly-once for pipelines where Kafka-to-Kafka or Flink state correctness matters (aggregations, billing counts). For external sinks, rely on idempotent writes and treat the pipeline as at-least-once into them. If latency matters more than duplicates, at-least-once with idempotent consumers is simpler.
numbers: Visibility latency: with a 10-second checkpoint interval, transactional sink output appears in roughly 10-second steps; shortening the interval reduces latency but adds checkpoint overhead.
pitfalls: Claiming exactly-once end to end while the sink is a non-idempotent HTTP call.
Downstream consumers using read_uncommitted and seeing aborted records.
Transaction timeouts shorter than checkpoint intervals, causing aborted transactions and data loss or stalls.
Using random ids generated during processing as idempotency keys; replay generates new ids. Keys must be deterministic from input.

followups.q: How do you write exactly-once into Postgres from Flink?
followups.a: Either a two-phase-commit sink that commits the database transaction on checkpoint completion, or idempotent upserts keyed by a deterministic id derived from the input, which is simpler and usually enough.

followups.q: Does Kafka exactly-once cover consumers in other services?
followups.a: Only if they participate in the transaction or dedupe themselves. A normal consumer that writes to its own database must be idempotent.

followups.q: What about sending emails from a stream?
followups.a: Emails can't be undone, so dedupe before sending: record the deterministic message id in a store and send with a provider idempotency key; accept a small risk window or confirm via provider status.

example: A billing pipeline aggregates usage events in Flink with exactly-once checkpoints and writes invoice line items into Kafka transactionally. The invoicing service consumes with read_committed and upserts line items by (customer, period, meter) so a replay never double-bills.
